content: Abfraction refers to the loss of tooth structure that occurs as a result of flexural forces acting on the teeth. Although this concept has not yet been definitively supported by dental research, it is hypothesized that enamel, particularly at the cementoenamel junction (CEJ), undergoes a specific pattern of destruction due to the separation of enamel rods. When teeth are subjected to flexion under pressure, the way teeth come into contact with each other—referred to as occlusion—creates tension on one side of the tooth and compression on the opposite side. This biomechanical stress is believed to result in V-shaped depressions on the side of the tooth experiencing tension and C-shaped depressions on the side under compression. However, this theory has not been universally accepted by researchers. One reason for skepticism is that many teeth experience occlusal forces that generate both tension and compression on either side, yet not all of these teeth exhibit signs of abfraction. If the theory were entirely accurate, a significantly larger number of teeth would be expected to show evidence of this type of structural damage, which is not observed in clinical practice. Ongoing research is being conducted to better understand the role of abfraction in this specific pattern of tooth destruction and to clarify its underlying mechanisms.
